name: Availability cascade
statement: An expressed perception gains plausibility through its own repetition in public, as people copy the beliefs of others and hide their doubts, until the consensus drives costly law.
meaning: Kuran and Sunstein put two known mechanisms together. An informational cascade runs when people with little private knowledge treat the apparent beliefs of others as evidence, so each new endorsement raises the next person's estimate. A reputational cascade runs on approval rather than evidence. People voice the view that will not get them criticised, and the missing dissent removes what would have slowed the process. Joined, and fed by the availability heuristic, the two make a perception more available in public discourse, and that availability is then read as support for it. Activists who work to start such a process are called availability entrepreneurs. The claim is about the compound, not about any of its parts. The availability heuristic has its own entry here, and its evidence does not carry over.

origin.who: Timur Kuran and Cass R. Sunstein
origin.note: The article ran in volume 51, issue 4, pages 683 to 768, and coins the term. Its footnote 3 lists the informational literature it builds on, naming Hirshleifer, Anderson and Holt, Arthur and Lane, Banerjee, Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch, and Mui, and then the reputational one, naming Akerlof and three earlier Kuran papers. The purpose is a policy argument rather than a finding. Part V proposes peer review, cost-benefit analysis, congressional risk oversight, a stronger role for the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, and a trusted Risk Information Site on the World Wide Web. The article wants that site run by a nongovernmental body along the lines of Consumer Reports. It says the federal government should take the lead only if no such body will, because a government-operated one would have a harder time rising above partisan politics. On product disparagement laws it identifies advantages and defends their constitutionality, then writes that doing so "is not, of course, to prove that on balance they are beneficial or desirable".

evidence: The article reports no data of its own. It is eighty-six pages of argument, one table and three narrated cases, and the cases are reconstructions from published accounts rather than measurements. Love Canal gets the longest treatment. Its footnote 19 names four sources, two Lois Gibbs memoirs, Landy, Roberts and Thomas on the Environmental Protection Agency, and Aaron Wildavsky's But Is It True?, then says the authors draw primarily on the two Gibbs memoirs and Wildavsky, with page citations omitted for readability. Alar rests on Wildavsky again. TWA Flight 800 rests on Robert Hahn's 1997 article in the Harvard Journal of Law and Public Policy, which the authors again say they draw on while avoiding a footnote for every fact. The brief for this entry named the Times Beach dioxin case as the third example. It is not one. The string Times Beach does not occur in the article, and dioxin occurs twice, both times inside the Love Canal narrative. The authors are explicit about what the cases are for. Footnote 101 says the examples were chosen because the data "nicely illustrate the phenomenon of regulatory action prompted by availability cascades rather than sound evidence", and that "nothing turns on the selected examples". A reader who thinks the science justified a given response is told the quarrel is with one interpretation and not with the argument. Footnote 18 makes the point as a joke: in convincing readers of the availability heuristic's significance the authors are exploiting the readers' reliance on it, and they "plead guilty". The conclusion lists seven claims the article has "tried to substantiate". Each is a proposition about mechanism, and none is attached to a measurement. The single table, headed Acceptability Effects, sets fifteen risk traits against the conditions that make each less acceptable, heavy media coverage among them, and carries no citation of its own beyond a footnote pointing to an alternative table in Margolis.

replication.headline: No study testing the availability cascade was located. The closest evidence tests its two halves separately, in settings with no risk, no regulator and no press.
replication.detail: The informational half has a laboratory literature. Anderson and Holt paid 72 subjects recruited from undergraduate economics courses at the University of Virginia $2 for each correct prediction to say in sequence which of two urns a private draw came from. Over all twelve sessions, cascades formed in 87 of 122 periods in which they were possible, 41 of 56 in the symmetric sessions and 46 of 66 in the asymmetric ones. Reverse cascades, where an early run of unrepresentative draws starts a chain of wrong guesses that later draws do not break, were about half as common as normal ones in both designs. Subjects made a decision consistent with their own draw rather than the Bayesian inference in 26 percent of the cases where the two conflicted, a figure from the symmetric sessions. Goeree, Palfrey, Rogers and McKelvey then ran much longer sequences, twenty or forty deciders across thirteen sessions at Caltech and UCLA, and found the cascades ephemeral. They form, collapse and re-form, and a reversal is more often than not self-correcting, in that the cascade switches from the incorrect to the correct state. Those readings come from Caltech Social Science Working Paper 1197 of April 2004 rather than the 2007 journal version, which could not be obtained. This site's information cascade entry treats that experiment at length. The reputational half has field evidence. Bursztyn, Gonzalez and Yanagizawa-Drott ran thirty-participant sessions with a sample of 500 married Saudi men aged 18 to 35, recruited from different neighbourhoods in Riyadh. Eighty-seven percent agreed in an anonymous online survey that women should be allowed to work outside the home, and about three-quarters underestimated how many of the other men in their session agreed. Correcting that belief raised the share who gave up a bonus payment to sign their wives up to a job-matching service by 9 percentage points, against 23 percent in the control group. Three to five months later their wives were 10 percentage points more likely to have applied for a job outside the home, from a baseline of 6 percent. Hale combined a nationally representative panel spanning Russia's post-Crimea rally with a list experiment and concluded that three quarters of those who rallied to Putin were engaging in at least some form of dissembling, and that the rally developed as a rapid cascade. Neither literature involves a risk judgement or a news cycle. The one study located that tracks a real scare as it runs is Frewer, Miles and Marsh, who collected attitude data before, during and after the surge in British reporting on genetically modified food in spring 1999. Risk perceptions rose and fell with the coverage, perceived benefit appeared permanently depressed afterwards, and trust in regulatory institutions was not affected. That study tests the social amplification of risk framework, which is a different and earlier proposal.

limits: Nothing above tests the composite claim, and it is not obvious what a test would look like. The cascade predicts the same public record as a genuine discovery: rising coverage, converging opinion, regulation. Telling them apart needs an independent verdict on the underlying risk, which is what the disputes are about. Searching on 21 September 2026 covered Crossref by bibliographic query, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, Europe PMC and general web search pairing the term with experiment, replication and empirical test. The article is cited widely and the citing work applies the term rather than testing it. Several things could not be read, and the reasons differ. Frewer, Miles and Marsh is the clearest case. Two indexes list it as open, and neither location holds the file: the Wageningen record carries metadata and a link to the publisher, and the East Anglia record says the full text is not available and offers a request-a-copy form. Wiley returns a Cloudflare interstitial rather than a paywall notice, so the block from here is a bot challenge. No sample size for that study appears in its abstract at the publisher, at PubMed or in either repository record. Combs and Slovic's 1979 content analysis, the usual citation for a correlation between newspaper coverage of causes of death and judged frequency, is closed at Sage and listed as having no open copy by Unpaywall, so no figure from it is repeated here. Wahlberg and Sjoberg's review of media and risk perception is closed at Taylor and Francis on the same terms. Goeree and colleagues' published article is closed at Oxford Academic, which returns a bot challenge, and the Caltech repository record for it holds only the experimental supplement. Wildavsky's book and the two Gibbs memoirs, which carry the article's factual account, sit in the Internet Archive's lending library and could not be borrowed, so the Love Canal and Alar narratives are reported as the article gives them. On the transmission step the whole argument rests on, the risk-perception literature is cooler than the article suggests. Sjoberg's 2000 abstract reports that heuristics and biases, mainly availability, account for only a minor portion of risk perception, that media contents have not been clearly implicated in it, and that the psychometric model, which he calls probably the leading contender, has explanatory value of only around 20 percent of the variance of raw data. Pachur's 2024 reanalysis covers three datasets, Lichtenstein and colleagues in 1978 with 74 participants, Hertwig and colleagues in 2005 with 45, and Pachur and colleagues in 2012 with 85. Media coverage overrepresented dramatic causes of death in all three, with the evidence very strong in two and inconclusive in the third when the dramatic and nondramatic categories rather than continuous drama ratings were used, at a Bayes factor of 1.87 for Hertwig. The matching distortion in people's frequency judgements appeared only in the 1978 data, at Bayes factors of 8.22 for category and 6.17 for ratings. Across the three datasets the pooled effect for category was 0.032, on a 95 percent highest density interval of minus 0.029 to 0.093, with a Bayes factor of 0.14 favouring its absence. That paper is treated at length in this site's availability heuristic entry.
misreadings: The cascade is not the availability heuristic. The heuristic is a claim about one person's judgement, and the cascade is a claim about what happens when many such judgements feed each other. The article draws the line itself in the TWA Flight 800 section, where it says an immediate reaction that makes millions of people independently detect a risk does not constitute an availability cascade. Its conclusion says the heuristic standing by itself leaves important gaps, so evidence for the first is not evidence for the second. The term is now used as a verdict on beliefs a writer rejects, and the article does not support that use. It states that a cascade reshaping public discourse may be socially beneficial and can draw overdue attention to neglected problems, and that there is no guarantee the effects will run either way. The Alar case is the weakest of the three as it is usually retold. Kuran and Sunstein report the agency's revised estimate of one child in 250,000 developing cancer, call it doubtless a nontrivial risk, and then cite Wildavsky for a United Nations panel finding even that figure too high. The same footnote names a competing view, a 1998 Washington Post piece by Rall and Landrigan claiming that the Alar episode was based on solid science. The EPA press release of 7 November 1989 announced that the agency intended to approve Uniroyal's request to cancel all food-use registrations of daminozide, and recorded that its May proposal rested on evidence that the breakdown product UDMH causes tumours in laboratory animals and that lifetime dietary exposure may result in an unacceptable risk to public health. Elliott Negin argued in Columbia Journalism Review in September 1996 that studies and reviews completed after the broadcast, including one by Uniroyal, confirmed the earlier ones the campaigners had relied on, attributing that to an EPA pesticides official. The magazine printed letters against him two months later. The response was disproportionate on the article's own numbers. It was not about nothing. Love Canal is the better case, and its strongest evidence arrived ten years after the article. Gensburg and colleagues followed 5,052 former residents through the New York State Cancer Registry from 1979 to 1996, over 76,496 person-years, and found 304 cancers. All sites combined gave a standardised incidence ratio of 0.95 against New York State, on a 95 percent interval of 0.83 to 1.05. Bladder and kidney cancers were raised, at 1.44 on an interval of 0.91 to 2.16 and 1.48 on an interval of 0.76 to 2.58. The authors write that the role of exposure to the landfill is unclear, and that further surveillance is warranted given the cohort's relatively young age.

sources.text: Kuran, T., & Sunstein, C. R. (1999). Availability cascades and risk regulation. Stanford Law Review, 51(4), 683-768. Full text read from the author's copy linked here, a scan of the JSTOR print; two downloads gave the same checksum. The DOI resolves to the JSTOR record.

Anderson, L. R., & Holt, C. A. (1997). Information cascades in the laboratory. American Economic Review, 87(5), 847-862. Full text read; source of the 72 subjects, the $2 per correct prediction, the 87 of 122 periods, the 41 of 56 and 46 of 66 splits and the 26 percent deviation rate. The copy at econweb.ucsd.edu cited here previously would not complete a TLS handshake on 21 September 2026; this copy was read instead.

Goeree, J. K., Palfrey, T. R., Rogers, B. W., & McKelvey, R. D. (2007). Self-correcting information cascades. Review of Economic Studies, 74(3), 733-762. Not obtained. Oxford Academic returns a bot challenge rather than an abstract, Unpaywall lists no open copy, and the Caltech repository record holds only the experimental supplement. Nothing above is taken from it; the working paper below was read instead.

Goeree, J. K., Palfrey, T. R., Rogers, B. W., & McKelvey, R. D. (2004). Self-correcting information cascades. California Institute of Technology Social Science Working Paper 1197, April 2004. Read in full. This is the working paper, not the 2007 journal article, and the two abstracts differ: the published one reports strong evidence for overweighting of private information, and this one does not use that wording. Source of the ephemeral cascades, the thirteen sessions at Caltech and UCLA and the sequences of twenty or forty deciders.

Bursztyn, L., Gonzalez, A. L., & Yanagizawa-Drott, D. (2020). Misperceived social norms: Women working outside the home in Saudi Arabia. American Economic Review, 110(10), 2997-3029. Full text read for the sample of 500, the 87 percent, the 9 percentage point sign-up effect against a control share of 23 percent, and the follow-up outcomes.

Hale, H. E. (2022). Authoritarian rallying as reputational cascade? Evidence from Putin's popularity surge after Crimea. American Political Science Review, 116(2), 580-594. Abstract read at Cambridge Core and again at Crossref, which agree word for word; the three-quarters figure comes from it. The full text is behind a purchase wall at Cambridge Core and Unpaywall lists no open copy, so it was not read.

Frewer, L. J., Miles, S., & Marsh, R. (2002). The media and genetically modified foods: Evidence in support of social amplification of risk. Risk Analysis, 22(4), 701-711. Abstract read in full at the Wageningen repository record linked here and at PubMed. The full text was not obtained on 21 September 2026: the Wageningen record holds no file, the East Anglia record says the full text is not available and offers a request-a-copy form, and Wiley returns a Cloudflare bot challenge. Sample sizes appear in none of these.

Kasperson, R. E., Renn, O., Slovic, P., Brown, H. S., Emel, J., Goble, R., Kasperson, J. X., & Ratick, S. (1988). The social amplification of risk: A conceptual framework. Risk Analysis, 8(2), 177-187. Abstract read in full at Crossref; cited for the framework the Frewer study tests. The full text was not read.

Sjoberg, L. (2000). Factors in risk perception. Risk Analysis, 20(1), 1-12. Abstract read in full at Crossref and at PubMed; source of the 20 percent of variance and of the statement that media contents have not been clearly implicated in risk perception. The full text was not obtained; Wiley returns a Cloudflare bot challenge and Unpaywall lists no open copy.

Pachur, T. (2024). The perception of dramatic risks: Biased media, but unbiased minds. Cognition, 246, 105736. Full text read from the published version deposited at the Max Planck Society repository, linked here; all Bayes factors and the pooled estimate above are read off it. ScienceDirect returns a bot challenge rather than a paywall, and the article is hybrid open access under CC BY-NC.

Gensburg, L. J., Pantea, C., Kielb, C., Fitzgerald, E., Stark, A., & Kim, N. (2009). Cancer incidence among former Love Canal residents. Environmental Health Perspectives, 117(8), 1265-1271. Full text read at PubMed Central for the cohort of 5,052, the 76,496 person-years, the 304 cancers, the standardised incidence ratios with their intervals and the conclusion. The publisher's own PDF at ehp.niehs.nih.gov is blocked by this session's egress policy.
US Environmental Protection Agency (1989). Daminozide (Alar) pesticide canceled for food uses. Press release, 7 November 1989. Read in full.

Negin, E. (1996). The Alar 'scare' was for real. Columbia Journalism Review, September/October 1996. Read in full as reprinted by PBS, which also carries the letters against it from the November/December 1996 issue. Disputes the standard retelling of the Alar episode.

Wahlberg, A. A. F., & Sjoberg, L. (2000). Risk perception and the media. Journal of Risk Research, 3(1), 31-50. Named here because it is the standing review of the question. Not read: Taylor and Francis returns a bot challenge, Unpaywall lists no open copy, and no repository copy was found on 21 September 2026.

Combs, B., & Slovic, P. (1979). Newspaper coverage of causes of death. Journalism Quarterly, 56(4), 837-849. Named here because it is the usual citation for the media-to-judgement correlation. Not read: Sage returns a bot challenge and Unpaywall lists no open copy, so no figure from it appears above. Crossref gives the pagination used here; the ERIC record gives it as 837-843 and 849.

Wildavsky, A. (1995). But Is It True? Harvard University Press. Named here because it carries the article's factual account of Love Canal and Alar, including the United Nations panel claim at page 221. Not read: the Internet Archive copy is lending-restricted, and the search-inside service is blocked by this session's egress policy.

Gibbs, L. M. (1982). Love Canal: My Story. State University of New York Press. Named here as one of the two memoirs the article draws on primarily for Love Canal.
